text: A Tokyo office worker watches a heist film, mistakes it for a record of real events, and begins planning her route to North Dakota. The error is never played for a laugh. What the film builds instead is the logic that makes it reasonable: a job that offers her nothing, and a fiction that offers a map with coordinates on it. Then it puts her in an American winter among strangers who are friendly and cannot understand the errand. David Zellner keeps to her point of view for 104 minutes and declines to translate her for anyone's comfort. The Sundance jury handed it a special prize, a strange fate for a film so committed to a woman being wrong and refusing correction. Obsession here is not an illness and not a metaphor. It is a plan, and she keeps to it.

Success has already happened by the time the film starts, and so has most of the damage. A punk musician is trying to stay sober and to find again whatever produced the songs that made her band matter, and the two projects turn out to be at odds, since the second has always run on the first one's fuel. Alex Ross Perry gives this 136 minutes, which is long, and the length is doing work: bandmates and everyone else still owed something, all of them kept waiting while one person decides what kind of day it will be. Music films usually organise themselves around a performance. This one takes the hours on either side of it, the part where a room fills with people managing someone. Sobriety, filmed seriously, is neither triumph nor relapse. It is a schedule that has to be kept.

Double Whammies sits beside a highway and sells drinks alongside a carefully policed idea of how a waitress should look. Lisa Conroy manages it, and manages the women on shift: their schedules, their crises, the small logistics of other people's lives. Andrew Bujalski compresses everything into one bad day and 91 minutes, which tethers the comedy to a clock — trouble arrives during a shift and is dealt with, or is not, before the next one starts. The film is interested in the labour of maintaining somebody else's fantasy: who keeps it presentable, who apologises for it, who gets sent home when it slips. Nothing is arranged so that management turns out to be secretly wise, and nothing is arranged so that the customers turn out to be monsters. Lisa's decency is a working method. The day tests whether a method is enough.

For a long stretch there is only walking: a couple who are engaged, the guide they have hired, and the Caucasus in every direction. They pass the hours with word games and stories, the kind of talk that demonstrates how well two people fit together. Julia Loktev shoots hiking as hiking — small bodies at the scale the mountains insist on — and lets the trust between them be established by pace and rhythm rather than by dialogue about the future. Somewhere in the 113 minutes there is a lapse lasting two or three seconds, after which the same trail, the same guide and the same itinerary belong to a different film. What follows is not a confrontation. It is an accounting conducted mostly in silence, between people with days of walking still ahead of them and nowhere else to be.

Land first, then people: a Scottish farm in the early 1900s, and the daughter of the house growing into the work of it. Terence Davies takes 135 minutes over this, and the length goes where a farming year actually goes — into seasons, repetition, the difference between a good harvest and a bad one. Coming of age on a holding like that is less a sequence of choices than a negotiation with what the ground and the household will permit; a daughter is labour before she is anything else, and whatever she wants has to be argued for against that. A film willing to spend its runtime on one life in one place is committing to duration instead of incident, and to history arriving late and secondhand. What it offers is texture: weather doing as it likes to a year's work, and a girl old enough to notice.

A theatre director asks a teenager to put her mother into the work: the arguments, the history, the parts that are not hers to hand over. Madeline has become integral to the troupe, which makes her useful, and the workshop's ambitions grow around her without quite asking permission. Josephine Decker builds the film from three women pulling at the same material — a mother who wants her daughter back, a director who wants a performance, and a girl who has just discovered that her own life is currency. Ninety-four minutes, and the wall between rehearsal room and household gives way in both directions. The discomfort is not that anyone is a villain. It is that the exercise plainly produces something, and that the producing of it protects everybody involved from having to name what it costs.

A camera bolted to the deck of a trawler loses the power to choose a subject. Lucien Castaing-Taylor's film, made off the New England coast with small waterproof cameras rigged to hulls, nets, gear and men, is built out of that surrender: the frame goes where the work goes and gets swamped when the work gets swamped. The industry is not explained. It is undergone — 87 minutes of chain and water and gulls, of angles no human operator could hold, of noise that arrives before any image is legible. The men register mostly as hands, oilskins and effort. Because the machinery outlasts anyone's attention, the argument gets made structurally: commercial fishing as a process that happens to involve people and does not slow down for them. Calling it a portrait is accurate roughly the way a sonar reading is a portrait.

Kirsten Johnson shot every frame of this for somebody else's film. Cameraperson is assembled out of what a career behind the lens accumulates: the footage around the usable takes, and the usable takes themselves, cut loose from the arguments they were gathered to support. Reframed, what becomes visible is the position of the person holding the camera — when she steadies it, when she pulls back, when she holds a shot for longer than the assignment required. The subject is the frame itself: what including something does to it, what leaving something out costs. Across 102 minutes the countries change and the hand does not. Documentary normally keeps that hand out of sight and treats the ethics of pointing a lens at a stranger as settled before shooting begins. Here it is the material.

At eighteen, Andrea Dunbar wrote a play about growing up on a Bradford estate and called it The Arbor. Clio Barnard's film takes the thirty years after: Dunbar's life and her death, the daughter, Lorraine, who inherited the setting without the writing, and a neighbourhood left holding a portrait of itself. It is filed as documentary and as drama at once, and that doubleness is the method — the testimony is real, the staging is not, and Barnard keeps both in view rather than picking one. Ninety-one minutes. Underneath sits a question about what a play does to the people whose lives it borrowed, and about who gets to speak in the next version. Lorraine is given room to talk at length, and the film does not tidy what she says into a lesson about a place.

Kris and Michal leave one party for another, and the camera goes with them until the light changes. Michał Marczak's film is filed as both documentary and drama, and the seam between the two is where it lives: the nights are real nights in a Polish city, the young men are themselves, and still the framing is too composed and the timing too lucky for anything here to have been merely caught. Sundance gave it a directing award in the documentary category, which is the most useful fact about it — a prize for arrangement, awarded to a film about drift. A hundred minutes of dancing, talk about love, streets emptying, the particular vanity of being young and awake while a city sleeps. Nothing accumulates into a plot. What accumulates is the sense of hours being spent, and of two people knowing they are spending them.

A marriage in Brooklyn is being audited from outside: a Nigerian couple, no child yet, and relatives keeping count. Andrew Dosunmu films that pressure as almost physical, a household where expectation arrives with the family and stays for dinner, and where a failure to conceive is treated as the wife's to answer for. The affection between the two of them is not in question; the arrangement around them is. Across 106 minutes the real difficulty is what cannot be said in the terms available — what the family will accept, what the community will notice, what a woman can propose without forfeiting her standing. The film moves toward a decision that could not have been discussed in advance, and it withholds judgment on the reasoning that produces one. Duty here is not an abstraction. It has names, and they are all in the room.

An actress reads everything available about a woman she has agreed to play, and the reading is the film. Kate Lyn Sheil is preparing to portray Christine Chubbuck, a Florida newscaster whose 1974 death was broadcast live, and Robert Greene points the camera at the preparation rather than at any finished performance: the research, the borrowed mannerisms, the drift from study into identification. It takes 112 minutes, and the unease builds along an unusual line, since every step toward understanding Chubbuck is also a step toward staging her for people who have come to watch. The film knows that about itself. What it refuses to hand over is the commodity a biographical drama exists to sell, which is an explanation of why a person did what she did.

Late summer to winter, 1993, from East Germany to Moscow: Chantal Akerman travelling east while the collapse was recent enough to still be visible in the stonework. Bullet holes from the last war are in the walls, the repairs have not been made, and the new arrangement has not arrived. What she films is waiting. Tracking shots down queues and platforms, slow circular pans, interiors held long enough to become inventories, Poles and Ukrainians and Germans and Russians sitting with a patience that was once a civic requirement and is now being spent on something nobody can name. Its place among the TSPDT thousand is odd for a film with almost no incident; the reason is duration. A hundred and fifteen minutes is long enough for looking to stop being observation and turn into something closer to obligation.

Two hundred and forty-four minutes, one autumn semester, one public university working out what it can still afford to be. Frederick Wiseman sits in the rooms where that gets decided: administrators going through budget shortfalls, teachers in front of classes, students arguing about tuition increases and about what a protest is supposed to accomplish. The length is not indulgence but method. An argument stated in full takes as long as it takes, and committee talk is allowed to run until the institution's shape emerges from procedure rather than from anyone's summary of it. Berkeley is filmed as a workplace with an idea attached to it, and by the fourth hour the two are hard to prise apart: the seminar and the payroll, the promise and the money, everyone in the building sincere and no one able to pay for all of it.
